newsitem.title: UK: Dividend, low debt may tempt Venezuela CANTV buyers.
newsitem.headline: Dividend, low debt may tempt Venezuela CANTV buyers.

text.p: Venezuela telephone company CANTV, gearing up for one of the biggest international offerings from Latin America this year, said on Friday it had eliminated one third of its debt and expected to offer a 12.5 percent dividend in 1998.

CANTV officials were in London at the end of a European roadshow to present the firm to foreign investors before the government sells most of its 49 percent stake in an international offering later this month.
It hopes to raise between $900 million and $1.0 billion in the process -- just under the $1.25 billion Telefonica del Peru made this year when Lima sold its stake.

CANTV is offering international investors American Depositary Shares, to be listed in New York and sold at an indicated price of $3.07 to $3.50 per share, and plans to offer a healthy dividend in just over a year's time.
"We expect to pay out a dividend in 1998 based on our results from 1997," CANTV's Chief Financial Officer Andres Glusky told investors at the presentation, which heads to the United States next week.
"We would have a minimum payout ratio of 12.5 percent in cash," he said, but added that no dividend can be paid until CANTV has paid off most of its debts and brings in sustainable earnings.

Pricing for the IPO will be announced on November 21 and trading will begin the next day, said Nick Millward, managing director of capital markets at SBC Warburg, which is joint global manager for the IPO with with Lehman Brothers.

The sale is seen as an important one for Venezuela after the setback earlier this year to the sale of Banco de Venezuela, which was suspended at the last minute when three chief bidders withdrew amid confusion over the handling of the auction.
Glusky said CANTV had been successful in reducing its heavy debt burden with foreign commercial banks.

"In less than two years our financial debt has been reduced by one third from $1.0 billion to less than $700 million, and the average life of the debt has been extended from 120 days in 1994 to almost four years today," he said.
"This year the firm should have $150 million outstanding -- we should burn that off in the first quarter of 1997."
CANTV president Gustavo Roosen said the firm enjoyed a positive relationship with independent regulator Conatel, and had exclusivity in local and international services until 2000.
Glusky said the firm was confident it could fund further development, which includes investment in new lines and digital transmission technology, through its cash flow.

An official from GTE Corp, leader of the VenWorld consortium which bought a 40 percent stake in the firm at $4.71 a share in 1991, said the consortium had achieved its aim in gaining strategic control of the firm.

"VenWorld has no reason to add to its investment because it has a strategic stake," he said. But he added other consortium members, including AT&T, would have to make individual decisions on whether to purchase more shares.

Investors at the roadshow kept their cards close to their chests, but one said this was a good chance to get exposure to the Venezuelan success story following the implementation this year of tough IMF reforms.

Earlier this week Bear Stearns forecast that the Venezuelan stock market index should nearly double by the end of next year, and one broker said CANTV would be a sure bet if that scenario were to materialise.
Another said that with little left to purchase on the debt side, purchasing CANTV shares would be a good way of adding Venezuela to one's book.
They said the firm stood a good chance of pushing the price to the upper end of the indicated range. --London Newsroom +44 171 542 2734
